note: Hand-authored landmark silhouettes for the 1940s Channel theatre (Phase 5 data input). Compiled by a Hermes agent from general world knowledge of the landmarks' real locations; no third-party dataset (no OSM extract, no gazetteer download) was used, so there is no licence encumbrance and no ATTRIBUTION.md change is required. lat/lon are real WGS84 decimal degrees (4 dp); 1 world unit = 1 m.

landmarks.name: Battersea Power Station
landmarks.from_air: A long brick mass along the river (GroundKit.box) capped by two tall ribbed, tapering chimneys (GroundKit.cyl, ~100 m) at one corner, with the unfinished shell of the B station alongside; reads as a huge horizontal block carrying two landmark stacks.
landmarks.era_note: Battersea A (two chimneys, 1933-35) was in service and B was begun in 1939 but stood unfinished through the war, so the 1940 silhouette has two chimneys (the famous four were not complete until 1955).

landmarks.name: Tower of London
landmarks.from_air: A squat square keep with four domed corner turrets (GroundKit.box) on a raised inner ward, ringed by a curtain wall studded with round mural towers (GroundKit.cyl) and four larger round corner towers; the four white turrets of the White Tower are the giveaway.
landmarks.era_note: The Tower was a working garrison, depot and POW site throughout 1939-45 (the Crown Jewels were removed for safe keeping).

landmarks.name: Westminster Abbey
landmarks.from_air: An enormous cruciform Gothic mass (GroundKit.box nave plus prism_mesh pitched roof) with two tall west towers (~69 m) and a lower central lantern, buttressed and pinnacled; reads as a vast stone church beside the Parliament clock tower.
landmarks.era_note: The Abbey (rebuilt from 1245) was the national coronation church and stood through the Blitz, losing only some roof lead to incendiaries.

landmarks.name: Royal Albert Hall
landmarks.from_air: A broad elliptical drum of red brick and terracotta (a wide, low GroundKit.cyl) under a shallow glazed saucer dome (flattened GroundKit.sphere), ringed by arched buttresses; an unmistakable oval arena-form hall, not a tower.
landmarks.era_note: Opened in 1871 and used for concerts and wartime rallies, the Hall survived the war intact.

landmarks.name: Crystal Palace (Sydenham towers and terraces)
landmarks.from_air: On the ridge stand the paired Brunel water towers, two tall tiered stone columns (stacked GroundKit.box and GroundKit.cyl) ~80 m high, above broad Italianate terraces and grand steps that still read as an empty formal plateau.
landmarks.era_note: The 1854 Crystal Palace itself burned in 1936, but its two water towers and terraces dominated Sydenham Hill until they were demolished in 1941 to deny bombers a landmark.

landmarks.name: Wembley Stadium (Empire Stadium twin towers)
landmarks.from_air: An oval bowl of terraces (a ring of GroundKit.box) with two square white entrance towers (~40 m) flanking the main front and a thin flagstaff above one; the twin-towers silhouette is the whole point.
landmarks.era_note: The 1923 Empire Stadium's Twin Towers stood throughout the war (the stadium was used for storage) and survived until 2003.

landmarks.name: London Docks (Wapping)
landmarks.from_air: A grid of long rectangular brick warehouses and granite quays (rows of GroundKit.box) with ranks of timber cranes and gasholders between deep rectangular water basins; reads as a dense industrial grid, not one building.
landmarks.era_note: The Port of London's Wapping and Royal basins were among the world's largest enclosed docks in 1940 and a prime Blitz target.

landmarks.name: County Hall, London
landmarks.from_air: A long, wide monumental block of pale stone (GroundKit.box) with a colonnaded river front and a low central dome, sitting on the embankment opposite the Houses of Parliament.
landmarks.era_note: The LCC County Hall (1922, its final wing opened 1939) was London's municipal seat and stood intact through the war.

landmarks.name: The Monument to the Great Fire of London
landmarks.from_air: A single fluted Doric column of pale stone (a tall GroundKit.cyl) on a moulded square pedestal, topped by a small gilt flame; a lone ~62 m column among the City rooftops.
landmarks.era_note: Wren's Monument (1677) survived the Blitz and stood over the burnt City district of 1940-41.

landmarks.name: Rochester Castle
landmarks.from_air: A tall square Norman keep (GroundKit.box) with clasping corner pilasters and a shallow pyramidal roof, on a mound above the Medway; the tallest of the square keeps in the Channel-theatre silhouette set.
landmarks.era_note: The 12th-century keep, still only about two-thirds of its intended height after the 1215 siege, dominated Rochester through the war.

landmarks.name: Rochester Cathedral
landmarks.from_air: A long Romanesque-Gothic nave (GroundKit.box plus prism_mesh roof) with a squat central tower and a tall flat-topped west front, lying low beside the castle keep across the street.
landmarks.era_note: Rochester Cathedral stood next to the Short Brothers aircraft works (a Luftwaffe target) and survived 1940-44.

landmarks.name: Leeds Castle
landmarks.from_air: A cluster of small stone towers and a keep (GroundKit.box plus GroundKit.cyl corner turrets) on an island inside a wide moat, ringed by a low curtain wall; a compact castellated island, not a big fortress.
landmarks.era_note: Leeds Castle (mainly 13th-16th century) was a private residence in 1940 and stood intact.

landmarks.name: Dover Castle Great Tower (the Keep)
landmarks.from_air: The great square keep (GroundKit.box with corner turrets and pilaster buttresses) on a raised mound inside the concentric castle, with the small octagonal Roman pharos (GroundKit.cyl) just beside it; a big crenellated cube above the cliffs.
landmarks.era_note: Dover's keep and the adjacent Roman Pharos formed the command area of the castle through Dunkirk and the Battle of Britain.

landmarks.name: Dover Admiralty Pier
landmarks.from_air: A long straight stone arm (~1 km, a low GroundKit.box) running into the Channel with a rounded pier-head, a small tower at its root and rails on the deck; reads as a single long spur of masonry.
landmarks.era_note: Dover's Admiralty Pier, the naval and military harbour arm, was central to the 1940 Dunkirk evacuation and to cross-Channel traffic through 1944.

landmarks.name: Hever Castle
landmarks.from_air: A small moated castle: a crenellated Tudor gatehouse and a modest tower (GroundKit.box with two small GroundKit.cyl turrets) inside a square moat, dwarfed by its gardens.
landmarks.era_note: Hever Castle (13th-century gatehouse plus Tudor manor house) was a private home in 1940 and stood intact.

landmarks.name: St Nicholas Church, New Romney
landmarks.from_air: A large medieval Cinque Port church: a long aisled nave (GroundKit.box plus prism_mesh roof) with a big square embattled tower at one end; reads as church-plus-tower among small houses.
landmarks.era_note: St Nicholas, New Romney, one of the Cinque Port churches, stood through the war (the port had already silted up centuries earlier, so it sits inland).

landmarks.name: St Mary's Church, Rye
landmarks.from_air: A cruciform church (GroundKit.box plus prism_mesh roof) with a heavy square tower carrying a gilded clock face, set on the hilltop above the town so both tower and nave break the skyline.
landmarks.era_note: St Mary's, Rye, a Cinque Port church, doubled as a fire watch and beacon tower, as it had in 1377.

landmarks.name: St Clement's Church, Sandwich
landmarks.from_air: A broad parish church: a long aisled nave (GroundKit.box plus prism_mesh roof) with a squat central tower, tucked inside the old Cinque Port town walls.
landmarks.era_note: St Clement's, Sandwich, a Cinque Port church, stood intact through 1939-45.

landmarks.name: Chatham Royal Dockyard
landmarks.from_air: A huge naval yard: long covered building slips and basin walls (rows of GroundKit.box), big rectangular dry docks and a forest of cranes and masts along the Medway; reads as an enormous shipyard grid.
landmarks.era_note: Chatham's royal dockyard built and repaired warships throughout the war and its sheds and basins drew Luftwaffe raids in 1940-41.

landmarks.name: Ramsgate Royal Harbour
landmarks.from_air: A large artificial harbour: two long stone breakwater arms (GroundKit.box) enclosing a near-circular basin, with a lighthouse on the west pier head; reads as a walled port cut into the coast.
landmarks.era_note: Ramsgate Royal Harbour, rebuilt 1810-1850, was England's only Royal Harbour and served as a naval base in 1940-44.

landmarks.name: Belfry of Saint-Eloi, Dunkirk
landmarks.from_air: A free-standing square brick belfry (a tall GroundKit.box) with a projecting clock stage and a small lantern turret (GroundKit.cyl) on top; a lone ~58 m tower beside the church.
landmarks.era_note: The 15th-century tower of Saint-Eloi was a landmark through the 1940 evacuation and the occupation (the church was badly damaged but the tower survived).

landmarks.name: Basilica of Notre-Dame, Boulogne-sur-Mer
landmarks.from_air: A large basilica crowned by a huge ribbed dome (~101 m, a flattened GroundKit.sphere over a GroundKit.cyl drum) rising above a long nave with two west towers; the dome dominates town and harbour alike.
landmarks.era_note: Notre-Dame de Boulogne's 19th-century basilica and great dome stood through the German occupation until it was gutted by Allied bombing in 1944.

landmarks.name: Column of the Grande Armee, Wimille
landmarks.from_air: A single tall stone Doric column (GroundKit.cyl) on a stepped base with a statue on top, standing alone in open ground; a lone ~53 m column north of the town.
landmarks.era_note: The Column of the Grande Armee (begun 1804, completed 1841) commemorating Napoleon's Army of England stood unaltered in 1940.

landmarks.name: Lille Hotel de Ville and Belfry
landmarks.from_air: A monumental red-brick and stone town hall (GroundKit.box) with a very tall detached belfry: a slender tower (~104 m) of stacked GroundKit.box and GroundKit.cyl stages, clock-staged, topped by a beacon lantern.
landmarks.era_note: Lille's 1921-32 Hotel de Ville and its 104 m belfry served as a German headquarters in 1940-44.

landmarks.name: Citadelle de Lille
landmarks.from_air: A huge star-shaped Vauban fortress: low bastioned ramparts with angular corner outworks (GroundKit.box walls) inside a wet moat and a plain massive gatehouse block at the centre.
landmarks.era_note: The 'Queen of Citadels' (1668-74, Vauban) guarded Lille and was garrisoned by occupying troops through 1940-44.

landmarks.name: Belfry of Ghent
landmarks.from_air: A tall square belfry of pale stone (a slender GroundKit.box) rising ~95 m, with corner turrets at the belfry stage and a small lantern on top; the tallest free-standing belfry in the Low Countries.
landmarks.era_note: Ghent's medieval belfry, with its 14th-century dragon and carillon, stood intact through 1940-44.

landmarks.name: Gravensteen, Ghent
landmarks.from_air: A compact stone castle: a big rectangular keep (GroundKit.box) with a ring of round corner towers (GroundKit.cyl) above a moat by the river, close to the belfry.
landmarks.era_note: The Gravensteen (Castle of the Counts, 1180) stood intact in 1940; its restoration came only after the war.

landmarks.name: Palais de Justice, Brussels
landmarks.from_air: An enormous law-court block on rising ground (a massive GroundKit.box with a central colonnade) capped by a great ribbed dome on a drum (GroundKit.cyl plus GroundKit.sphere); one of Europe's largest 19th-century buildings.
landmarks.era_note: The 1883 Palais de Justice (Poelaert) was the largest building in Europe and dominated Brussels through the occupation.

landmarks.name: Brussels Town Hall
landmarks.from_air: A tall slender Gothic town-hall tower (~96 m) of stacked GroundKit.box and GroundKit.cyl stages with a spire of openwork pinnacles, springing above an ornate lower hall on the Grand-Place.
landmarks.era_note: Brussels Town Hall (1402-1455) and its 96 m tower dominated the Grand-Place throughout the occupation.

landmarks.name: Antwerp Kattendijk Docks
landmarks.from_air: Miles of straight quays (GroundKit.box walls) lining huge rectangular wet docks, with a forest of tall cranes, grain elevators and gantry sheds along the banks; the whole river bank reads as an endless grid of docks.
landmarks.era_note: Antwerp's Kattendijk and Noorder docks were among Europe's busiest in 1940 and later the objective of the 1944 Scheldt campaign.

landmarks.name: Zeebrugge Mole
landmarks.from_air: A long straight breakwater arm (a low GroundKit.box) running roughly 2.5 km into the sea with a lighthouse and a harbour-entrance gap, walling off a vast artificial basin.
landmarks.era_note: The Zeebrugge Mole (completed 1907) and its harbour were used as a German U-boat and small-craft base in 1940-44.

landmarks.name: Rotterdam Maashaven Docks
landmarks.from_air: Immense rectangular docks (rows of GroundKit.box quays) with grain elevators, cranes and shipyard slips along the Maas; reads as a huge water-anchored industrial grid on the south bank.
landmarks.era_note: Rotterdam's Maashaven and Waalhaven were among the world's largest dock works in 1940, largely bombed flat in the May 1940 attack and rebuilt.

landmarks.name: Ostend Harbour
landmarks.from_air: A compact harbour with two pier breakwaters (paired GroundKit.box arms) enclosing a tidal basin, a fish quay and a small lighthouse, backed by long seafront terrace blocks.
landmarks.era_note: Ostend's harbour was a German small-craft base in 1940-44 and was bombed repeatedly.

landmarks.name: Hohenzollern Bridge, Cologne
landmarks.from_air: A long iron bowstring bridge (a row of GroundKit.box arch members over stone piers) leading dead straight to the cathedral, with an equestrian statue on the left-bank abutment; a flat deck carried on high steel arches.
landmarks.era_note: The 1911 Hohenzollern Bridge carried all rail traffic across the Rhine at Cologne until it was dropped into the river in 1945.

landmarks.name: Gross St. Martin, Cologne
landmarks.from_air: A Romanesque church on the river bank whose great central tower is a square base with four round corner turrets and conical caps (GroundKit.box plus GroundKit.cyl prisms); a dense cluster of roofs and towers at the water's edge.
landmarks.era_note: Gross St. Martin (12th-13th century), directly opposite the cathedral, stood until it was bombed in 1944.

landmarks.name: Deutsches Eck, Koblenz
landmarks.from_air: A towering equestrian monument on a stepped stone podium (a big GroundKit.box) at the tip of a spit where the Rhine and Moselle meet, topped by a bronze horseman on a tall column; a lone vertical at the confluence.
landmarks.era_note: The 1897 Deutsches Eck monument to Kaiser Wilhelm I was intact through 1940-44 (its bronze statue was removed only in 1945).

landmarks.name: Palais des Princes-Eveques, Liege
landmarks.from_air: A vast palace built around two courtyards (two big GroundKit.box ranges with long window rows), its front a fortified wall with a sturdy central gate tower; a squat, broad princely block above the Meuse.
landmarks.era_note: Liege's Prince-Bishops' Palace (the present building begun 1526) was the city's administrative seat and stood through 1940-44.

landmarks.name: Birmingham Town Hall
landmarks.from_air: A Greek-temple concert hall (a long GroundKit.box on a stepped base) with a row of tall Corinthian columns and a raised pediment-topped portico fronting an open square; a classical temple among smoky factories.
landmarks.era_note: Birmingham Town Hall (1834) stood through the Blitz, closed since 1936 and used as a store, and survived largely intact.

landmarks.name: Birmingham Council House
landmarks.from_air: A long Renaissance-revival block (GroundKit.box) with a pedimented central bay, a small corner dome and a tall flagstaff; a broad classical civic front on the city-centre square.
landmarks.era_note: Birmingham Council House (1879, extended 1911) stood on Victoria Square through the war.

landmarks.name: Holy Trinity Church Spire, Coventry
landmarks.from_air: A slender 14th-century spire (a tapering GroundKit.cyl) on a square tower above a broad parish church; one of Coventry's Three Spires, standing alone over the burnt-out city.
landmarks.era_note: Holy Trinity's ~72 m spire, one of the Three Spires, stood intact amid the 1940 Coventry Blitz ruins.

landmarks.name: Coventry Council House
landmarks.from_air: A long neo-Georgian civic block (GroundKit.box) with a central portico and a small clock tower at one end, fronting a wide street.
landmarks.era_note: Coventry Council House (1917) fronted the city centre and stood through the Blitz.

landmarks.name: Nottingham Council House
landmarks.from_air: A broad classical civic block (GroundKit.box) with a long colonnade and a big ribbed dome (GroundKit.cyl plus GroundKit.sphere) rising above the roof, on the edge of a large market square.
landmarks.era_note: Nottingham's 1929 Council House and its dome dominated Old Market Square through 1940-44.

landmarks.name: Martello tower (Kent / Sussex coast)
landmarks.from_air: A squat, battered round masonry tower (a wide tapered GroundKit.cyl) with a flat parapeted gun platform, a ring of dark embrasures and a low doorway; a lone masonry drum among the shingle and saltmarsh.
landmarks.era_note: The Martello towers of the 1805-1812 coast defence line (Dymchurch, Sandgate, Pevensey, Eastbourne) served as coast-defence and signal posts through 1940-45.

landmarks.name: HM Coastguard station
landmarks.from_air: A two-storey white watch house with a gabled roof, a glazed lookout turret and a flagstaff on the seaward end, with a rocket / boathouse shed alongside; a small look-out post on the cliff.
landmarks.era_note: HM Coastguard stations along the Channel coast were manned watch posts through 1939-45, reporting shipping and invasion alerts.

landmarks.name: RNLI lifeboat station
landmarks.from_air: An open boathouse with a wide doorway and its launching slipway running out over the shingle, a crew / lookout room beside it and a lifebuoy on a post; the boat ready on its carriage.
landmarks.era_note: The RNLI lifeboat stations of the Channel ports (Dover, Ramsgate, Newhaven, Hastings, Eastbourne) launched throughout the 1940 war to shipping and downed aircrew.

landmarks.name: Seaside lido
landmarks.from_air: A long rectangular open-air pool of pale concrete in a paved terrace, with diving boards at one end, a fountain jet in the middle and a low changing-room block along the landward side.
landmarks.era_note: The 1930s seaside lidos (Saltdean, Tinside, Brighton) were commandeered during the war for military training and recreation, many with their pools drained.

landmarks.name: Seaside bandstand
landmarks.from_air: A raised octagonal platform on slim iron columns under a shallow domed metal roof with a finial, ringed by a pierced valance railing with a short flight of steps; a small circular dot on the promenade.
landmarks.era_note: The Victorian and Edwardian seaside bandstands (Eastbourne, Brighton) stood on the promenade through 1939-45; several doubled as rallying and concert points.

landmarks.name: Requisitioned holiday camp
landmarks.from_air: A grid of small rows of identical chalets (GroundKit.box) around a large central hall / dining block with a flagstaff and a gatehouse; a dense regular camp pattern unlike a village.
landmarks.era_note: The seaside holiday camps (Butlin's Clacton and Dovercourt Bay, Corton) were requisitioned in 1940 as military camps and transit depots, many ringed with barbed wire.
